source_text: Est ergo deus pater omnium institutor et creator, solus originem nesciens, inuisibilis, immensus, immortalis, aeternus, unus deus; cuius neque magnitudini neque maiestati neque uirtuti quicquam, non dixerim praeferri, sed nec comparari potest. ex quo, quando ipse uoluit, sermo filius natus est: qui non in sono percussi aeris, aut tono coactae de uisceribus uocis accipitur, sed in substantia prolatae a deo uirtutis agnoscitur. cuius sacrae et diuinae natiuitatis arcana nec apostolus didicit, nec prophetes comperit, nec angelus sciuit, nec creatura cognouit; filio soli nota sunt, qui patris secreta cognoulit. Hic ergo, cum sit genitus a patre, semper est in patre. semper autem sic dico, ut non innatum, sed natum probem. sed qui ante omne tempus est, semper in patre fuisse dicendus est: nec enim tempus illi assignari potest, qui ante Semper enim in patre, ne pater non semper sit quia ‘et pater illum etiam praecedit, quod necesse est quoniam antecedat necesse est eum, qui habet originem, ille qui originem nescit; simul ut hic minor sit, dum in illo esse se scit, habens originem, quia nascitur, et per patrem quodam modo, quamuis originem habet, qua nascitur, uicinus in natiuitate, dum ex eo patre, qui originem solus non habet, nascitur. hic ergo quando pater uoluit, processit ex patre: et qui in patre fuit, quia ex patre fuit, cum patre postmodum fuit, quia ex patre processit, substantia scilicet illa diuina, cuius nomen est uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil. omnia enim post ipsum sunt, quia per ipsum sunt, et merito ipse est ante omnia, sed post patrem, quando per illum facta sunt omnia. qui processit ex eo, ex cuius uoluntate facta sunt omnia, deus utique procedens ex deo, secundam personam efficiens post patrem, qua filius, sed non eripiens illud patri, quod unus est deus. Si enim natus non fuisset, innatus comparatus cum eo qui esset innatus, aequatione in utroque ostensa, duos faceret innatos, et ideo duos faceret deos. si non genitus esset, collatus cum eo qui genitus non esset, et aequales inuenti, duos deos merito reddidissent non geniti; atque ideo duos Christus reddidisset deos. si sine origine esset ut pater, inuentus et ipse principium omnium ut pater, duo faciens principia, duos ostendisset nobis consequenter et deos. aut si et ipse filius non esset, sed pater generans de se alterum filium, merito collatus cum patre et tantus denotatus, duos patres effecisset, et ideo duos approbasset etiam deos. si inuisibilis fuisset, cum inuisibili collatus, par expressus, duos inuisibiles ostendisset, et ideo duos comprobasset et deos. si incomprehensibilis, si et cetera quaecumque sunt patris, merito, dicimus, duorum deorum quam isti confingunt controuersiam suscitasset. nunc autem quicquid est, non ex se est, quia nec innatus est, sed ex patre est, quia genitus est. siue dum uerbum est, siue dum uirtus est, siue dum sapientia est, siue dum lux est, siue dum filius est, et quicquid horum est, dum non aliunde est, quam, sicut diximus iam superius, ex patre, patri suo originem suam debens, discordiam diuinitatis de numero duorum deorum facere non potuit, qui ex illo, qui est unus deus, originem nascendo contraxit. quo genere, dum et unigenitus est et primogenitus ex illo est qui, quia originem non habet, unus est omnium rerum et principium et caput, idcirco unum deum asseruit, quem non sub ullo principio aut initio, sed initium potius et principium rerum omnium comprobauit. Idem est denique quod nihil ex arbitrio suo gerit, nec ex consilio suo facit, nec a se uenit, sed imperiis paternis omnibus et praeceptis oboedit: ut quamuis probet illum natiuitas filium, tamen morigera oboedientia asserat illum paternae uoluntatis, ex quo est, ministrum. ita dum se patri in omnibus obtemperantem reddit, quamuis sit et deus, unum tamen deum patrem de oboedientia sua ostendit, ex quo et originem traxit. Et ideo duos deos facere non potuit, quia nec duas origines fecit, qui ex eo, qui originem non habet, principium natiuitatis ante omne tempus accepit. nam cum id sit principium ceteris quod innatum est (quod deus solus pater est, qui extra originem est, ex quo hic est qui natus est), dum qui ex illo nascitur merito ex eo uenit, qui originem non habet, principium probans illud esse, ex quo ipse est, etiamsi deus est qui natus est, unum tamen deum ostendit, quem hic qui natus est esse sine origine comprobauit. Est ergo deus, sed in hoc ipsum genitus, ut esset deus. est et dominus, sed in hoc ipsum natus ex patre, ut esset dominus. est et angelus, sed ad annuntiandum magnum dei consilium €x patre suo angelus destinatus. cuius sic diuinitas traditur, ut non aut dissonantia aut inaequalitate diuinitatis duos deos reddidisse uideatur. subiectis enim ei quasi filio omnibus rebus a patre, dum ipse cum his, quae illi subiecta sunt, patri suo subicitur, patris quidem sui filius probatur; ceterorum autem et dominus et deus esse reperitur. ex quo dum huic qui est deus omnia substrata traduntur, et cuncta sibi subiecta filius accepta refert patri, totam diuinitatis auctoritatem rursus patri remittit. unus deus ostenditur uerus et aeternus pater, a quo solo haec uis diuinitatis emissa, etiam in filium tradita et directa, rursum substantiae per communionem ad patrem reuoluitur. deus quidem ostenditur filius, cui diuinitas tradita et porrecta conspicitur; et tamen nihilominus unus deus pater probatur, dum gradatim reciproco meatu illa maiestas atque diuinitas ad patrem, qui dederat eam, rursum ab illo ipso filio missa reuertitur et retorquetur; ut merito deus pater omnium deus sit, et principium ipsius quoque filii sui, quem dominum genuit: filius autem ceterorum omnium deus sit, quoniam omnibus illum deus pater praeposuit, quem genuit. ita mediator dei et hominum Christus Iesus, omnis creaturae subiectam sibi habens a patre proprio potestatem, qua deus est, cum tota creatura subdita sibi, concors patri suo deo inuentus, unum et solum et uerum deum patrem suum, manente in illo quod etiam auditus est, breuiter approbauit.
thought_title: God the Father and the Son
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, God the Father is the institutor and creator of all, alone not knowing origin, invisible, immense, immortal, eternal, one God; to whose magnitude, or majesty, or power, nothing can be preferred, nor even compared. From whom, when He Himself willed, the Son, the Word, was born: who is not received in the sound of struck air, or in the tone of forced voice from the viscera, but is recognized in the substance of the power produced by God. The secrets of whose sacred and divine birth, neither the apostle learned, nor the prophet discovered, nor the angel knew, nor any creature perceived; they are known to the Son alone, who knew the Father's secrets. This Son, therefore, when He is born from the Father, is always in the Father. I say always, so that I may prove not that He is innate, but that He is born. But He who is before all time must be said to have always been in the Father: for time cannot be assigned to Him who is before all time. For the Father is always, lest the Father not always be, because He also precedes the Son, as it is necessary that He precede Him who has an origin, He who does not know origin; at the same time, the Son is lesser, while He knows that He exists in the Father, having an origin, because He is born, and through the Father, in some way, although He has an origin, by which He is born, He is near in birth, while He is born from the Father, who alone does not have an origin. Therefore, when the Father willed, the Son proceeded from the Father: and He who was in the Father, because He was from the Father, was afterwards with the Father, because He proceeded from the Father, that divine substance, whose name is the Word, through which all things were made, and without which nothing was made. For all things are after Him, because they are through Him, and rightly He is before all things, but after the Father, when all things were made through Him. He who proceeded from Him, from whose will all things were made, is certainly God proceeding from God, making a second person after the Father, which is the Son, but not taking away from the Father what is His, that He is one God. If He had not been born, compared to Him who is innate, the equality shown in both would have made two innates, and therefore two Gods. If He had not been generated, compared to Him who is not generated, and found equal, they would have rightly made two ungenerated Gods; and therefore Christ would have made two Gods. If He were without origin, like the Father, and found to be the principle of all, like the Father, He would have made two principles, and consequently shown us two Gods. Or if He Himself were not the Son, but the Father generating another Son from Himself, compared to the Father and designated as so great, He would have made two Fathers, and therefore approved two Gods. If He were invisible, compared to the invisible, expressed as equal, He would have shown two invisibles, and therefore approved two Gods. If He were incomprehensible, or whatever other things are of the Father, rightly, we say, the controversy of two Gods, which they invent, would have arisen. But now, whatever He is, He is not from Himself, because He is not innate, but from the Father, because He is generated. Whether as the Word, or as power, or as wisdom, or as light, or as the Son, and whatever of these He is, as long as He is not from elsewhere, but from the Father, as we said above, owing His origin to His Father, He could not make a discord of divinity, making two Gods, who, being born from the one God, contracted origin. By what kind, while He is both only-begotten and first-begotten from Him, who, because He does not have an origin, is one and the principle and head of all things, therefore He asserted one God, whom He did not place under any principle or beginning, but rather the beginning and principle of all things. Finally, He does nothing by His own will, nor does He do anything by His own counsel, nor does He come from Himself, but He obeys all the Father's commands and precepts: so that, although His birth proves Him to be the Son, yet His obedient subjection asserts Him to be the minister of the Father's will, from whom He is. Thus, while He renders Himself obedient to the Father in all things, although He is also God, He shows that there is one God, the Father, by His obedience, from whom He originated. And therefore, He could not make two Gods, because He did not make two origins, who received the principle of birth before all time from Him who does not have an origin. For since what is innate is the principle of other things (which God the Father alone is, who is outside origin, from whom this one is who is born), while He who is born from Him rightly comes from Him who does not have an origin, proving that principle to be from which He Himself is, even if He is God who is born, He shows that there is one God, whom this one who is born proved to be without origin. Therefore, He is God, but in this, that He is born, so that He may be God. He is also Lord, but in this, that He is born from the Father, so that He may be Lord. He is also an angel, but destined to announce the great counsel of God from His Father. The divinity of whom is handed down in such a way that it does not seem to have made two Gods by a discord or inequality of divinity. For when all things are subjected to Him as to a Son by the Father, while He Himself is subjected to His Father with the things that are subjected to Him, He is proved to be the Father's Son; and He is found to be the Lord and God of other things. From which, when all things are given to Him who is God, and the Son receives all things subjected to Himself and refers them to the Father, He again remits the whole authority of divinity to the Father. One God is shown, the true and eternal Father, from whom alone this power of divinity is sent, and also given and directed to the Son, and again returns to the Father through communion of substance. The Son is shown to be God, to whom the divinity is given and extended; and yet, nonetheless, one God, the Father, is proved, while the majesty and divinity gradually return to the Father, who gave it, and are again sent back and turned by the Son Himself; so that rightly, God the Father is the God of all, and the principle of His own Son, whom He generated as Lord: but the Son is the God of all other things, because God the Father has placed Him, whom He generated, over all things. Thus, Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men, having all creation subjected to Himself by the Father's own power, by which He is God, with all creation subjected to Himself, is found to be in harmony with His Father, God, and briefly approved one and only true God, His Father, remaining in what has also been heard.

pass_b_english: God the Father is the institutor and creator of all, alone in not knowing origin, invisible, immense, immortal, eternal, the one God; nothing can be preferred to his magnitude or majesty or power, nor even compared. When he himself willed, the Son, the Word, was born from him: he is not perceived in the sound of struck air or in the tone of a voice forced from the viscera, but is recognized in the substance of the power brought forth from God. The secrets of his sacred and divine birth were not learned by the apostle, nor discovered by the prophet, nor known by the angel, nor perceived by any creature; they are known to the Son alone, who knew the Father's secrets (John 1:1-3).

Therefore, because he is born from the Father, the Son is always in the Father. I say 'always' so that I may prove not that he is innate, but that he is born. Yet he who is before all time must be said to have always been in the Father, for time cannot be assigned to him who is before all time. The Father is always, lest the Father not always be, because he also precedes the Son, as it is necessary that he precede the one who has an origin, since he himself does not know origin; at the same time the Son is lesser, while he knows that he exists in the Father, having an origin because he is born, and through the Father, in a certain way, although he has an origin by which he is born, he is near in birth, while he is born from the Father who alone does not have an origin.

He who proceeded from him, from whose will all things were made, is certainly God proceeding from God, making a second person after the Father, which is the Son, but not taking away from the Father that which is his, that he is one God.

If he had not been born, the innate one compared with him who would be innate, the equality shown in both would have made two innates, and therefore would have made two Gods. If he had not been generated, compared with him who was not generated, and found equal, they would have rightly made two ungenerated Gods; and therefore Christ would have made two Gods. If he were without origin like the Father, and were found to be the principle of all like the Father, he would have made two principles, and consequently would have shown us two Gods. Or if he himself were not the Son, but the Father generating another Son from himself, compared with the Father and designated as so great, he would have made two Fathers, and therefore would have approved two Gods even. If he were invisible, compared with the invisible, expressed as equal, he would have shown two invisibles, and therefore would have proved two Gods. If he were incomprehensible, or whatever other attributes belong to the Father, rightly, we say, the controversy of two Gods which they invent would have arisen.

But now, whatever he is, he is not from himself, because he is not innate, but from the Father, because he is generated. Whether as the Word, or as power, or as wisdom, or as light, or as the Son, and whatever of these he is, as long as he is not from elsewhere but from the Father, as we said above, owing his origin to his Father, he could not make a discord of divinity by making two Gods, who, being born from the one God, contracted origin. For since what is innate is the principle of other things (which God the Father alone is, who is outside origin, from whom this one is who is born), while he who is born from him rightly comes from him who does not have an origin, proving that principle to be the one from which he himself is, even if he is God who is born, he shows that there is one God, whom this one who is born proved to be without origin. For when all things are subjected to him as to a Son by the Father, while he himself is subjected to his Father with the things that are subjected to him, he is proved to be the Father's Son; and he is found to be the Lord and God of other things. Thus Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men, having all creation subjected to himself by the Father's own power, by which he is God, with all creation subjected to himself, is found to be in harmony with his Father God, and briefly approved one and only and true God, his Father, remaining in what has also been heard.
